notable_absence.finding: The page states 'Roles, like users, have to be explicitly created by an administrator' - the same fact already captured elsewhere in the registry as sgw:role createdVia sgw:admin-rest-api - but this page never names the Admin REST API specifically, only 'an administrator', so this record does not re-assert createdVia with this page's weaker wording as evidence. Also notable and NOT modeled as a relation: 'Nonexistent roles don't cause an error, but have no effect on the user's access privileges' and 'You can create roles retrospectively. As soon as a role is created, any pre-existing references to it take effect' - a forward-reference/lazy-binding tolerance with no equivalent stated for access()'s username argument or requireRole()'s rolename argument anywhere in this batch. No promoted predicate captures 'silently tolerates a forward reference to a not-yet-existing object', so this is recorded as a finding only.

cross_component_finding: role()'s rolename argument uses the SAME 'role:' prefix requirement as requireRole()'s (round 3, already promoted as appliesToRoleWhenPrefixed) - both throw if the prefix is missing. This is a MANDATORY convention (throws if absent) applied to a dedicated rolename argument, in contrast to access()'s OPTIONAL use of the same prefix on its polymorphic username argument (where the prefix, if present, redirects the grant from a user to a role, but its absence is not an error - it just means 'this is a user'). The convention is therefore one lexical rule serving two different roles in the API: a disambiguator on access()'s single overloaded argument, versus a mandatory validity constraint on role()'s and requireRole()'s dedicated rolename argument. Both are modeled with the same promoted predicate (appliesToRoleWhenPrefixed) since the underlying convention is identical, but the optional-vs-mandatory distinction is worth flagging for reconciliation in case a future round wants two predicates instead of one.
